course.title: Real Analysis
course.description: The rigorous foundations under calculus - the completeness of the real numbers, limits of sequences and functions, continuity, differentiation, integration, and uniform convergence, all built from careful definitions and full proofs. Structure adapted from MIT OpenCourseWare 18.100 Real Analysis (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: The least upper bound (supremum) of a set S is...
options: the smallest number that is greater than or equal to every element of S
the average of the elements of S
questions.explanation: The supremum is the least of all upper bounds; it need not belong to S - see 'The real numbers and completeness'.

questions.prompt: The completeness property of the real numbers says that...
options: every nonempty set bounded above has a supremum in the reals
questions.explanation: Completeness (the least-upper-bound property) is what distinguishes the reals from the rationals.

questions.prompt: A sequence a_n converges to L means that for every epsilon > 0 there exists N such that...
options: |a_n - L| < epsilon for all n > N
questions.explanation: Convergence pins the tail of the sequence inside every epsilon-band around L - see 'Sequences and their limits'.

questions.prompt: A function f is continuous at a point a if for every epsilon > 0 there is a delta > 0 such that...
questions.explanation: This is the epsilon-delta definition of continuity at a point.

questions.prompt: The derivative of f at a is defined as...
options: the limit of (f(x) - f(a)) / (x - a) as x approaches a, when it exists
the slope of any secant line
questions.explanation: The derivative is the limit of difference quotients - see 'Differentiation and the mean value theorem'.

questions.prompt: The geometric series 1 + r + r^2 + r^3 + ... converges exactly when...
questions.explanation: For |r| < 1 the partial sums approach 1 / (1 - r); otherwise the terms do not shrink to 0.

questions.prompt: The intermediate value theorem requires the function to be...
questions.explanation: Continuity on a closed interval is exactly what guarantees every intermediate value is attained.

questions.prompt: A sequence whose terms eventually stay arbitrarily close to each other is called...
questions.explanation: A Cauchy sequence has |a_m - a_n| small for all large m and n - see 'Cauchy sequences and convergence'.

lessons.title: The real numbers and completeness (sup and inf)
lessons.grammar_note: An upper bound need not lie in the set, and the supremum need not be attained: sup of the open interval (0, 1) is 1, yet 1 is not in the set.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the least-upper-bound property, compute the supremum and infimum of a set, and prove a number is the supremum using its two defining properties. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what makes the supremum the *least* of all upper bounds?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An upper bound of a set S is a number M with x less than or equal to M for every x in S. The supremum, written sup S, is the least upper bound: it is an upper bound, and no smaller number is an upper bound. Symmetrically, the infimum inf S is the greatest lower bound. The completeness axiom of the real numbers states that every nonempty set that is bounded above has a supremum that is itself a real number. This single property is what the rationals lack: the set of rationals whose square is less than 2 is bounded above but has no rational least upper bound, while in the reals its supremum is the square root of 2. A clean working test: M = sup S exactly when (1) x less than or equal to M for all x in S, and (2) for every epsilon > 0 there is some x in S with x > M - epsilon.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: For S = (0, 1), every x satisfies x < 1, so 1 is an upper bound; and for any epsilon > 0 the number 1 - epsilon/2 lies in S and exceeds 1 - epsilon, so no smaller bound works. Hence sup S = 1, though 1 is not in S. Likewise inf S = 0. For the set {1 - 1/n : n = 1, 2, 3, ...} = {0, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, ...}, every term is below 1, and the terms climb toward 1, so sup = 1 (never attained) while inf = 0 (attained at n = 1). To prove sup of {x rational : x^2 < 2} equals the square root of 2, one checks both defining properties: it is an upper bound because x^2 < 2 forces x < sqrt(2), and nothing smaller is an upper bound because between any smaller number and sqrt(2) there sits a rational with square below 2.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is sup of the closed interval [2, 5]? Is it attained? 2) What is inf of {1/n : n = 1, 2, 3, ...}? Is it attained? 3) Give an upper bound of (0, 3) that is not the supremum. 4) True or false: the supremum of a set always belongs to the set. 5) State the two properties you must verify to show M = sup S. Answers: 1) 5, and it is attained since 5 is in the set. 2) inf = 0, not attained, since 1/n stays positive but drops below every epsilon > 0. 3) any number greater than 3, for example 4 (or 3 itself). 4) False, as (0, 1) shows. 5) M is an upper bound, and for every epsilon > 0 some element exceeds M - epsilon.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming sup S must be an element of S; it often is not, as with an open interval. Mistake: confusing 'an upper bound' with 'the least upper bound' - many numbers bound a set, but only one is the supremum. Exit: (a) What property of the reals guarantees sup S exists whenever S is nonempty and bounded above? (b) What is inf of the open interval (0, 1)? Answers: completeness (the least-upper-bound property); 0, which is not attained.

lessons.title: Sequences and their limits
lessons.grammar_note: Read the limit definition in order: epsilon is chosen first by an adversary, then you must produce N depending on epsilon - never the reverse.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write the epsilon-N definition of a limit, prove a specific sequence converges by producing N from epsilon, and apply the limit laws and the squeeze theorem. Warm-up: how large must n be so that 1/n < 0.01?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A sequence a_n converges to a limit L if for every epsilon > 0 there exists a natural number N such that |a_n - L| < epsilon for all n > N. In words: no matter how narrow the band (L - epsilon, L + epsilon), the sequence eventually enters that band and stays there. The number N is allowed to depend on epsilon; smaller epsilon usually forces larger N. Convergent sequences are bounded, and limits are unique. The limit laws let you split lim of a sum, product, or quotient (with a nonzero denominator limit) into the separate limits. The squeeze theorem says that if a_n is trapped between b_n and c_n which both converge to L, then a_n converges to L as well. A monotone sequence that is bounded always converges - this is a direct consequence of completeness, since its limit is the supremum (or infimum) of its terms.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Claim: lim of 1/n = 0. Given epsilon > 0, choose N to be any integer greater than 1/epsilon. Then for n > N we have 1/n < 1/N < epsilon, so |1/n - 0| < epsilon. That is the whole proof. Limit laws: lim of (3 + 1/n) = 3 + 0 = 3, and lim of ((2n + 1)/n) = lim of (2 + 1/n) = 2. Squeeze: since -1/n less than or equal to (sin n)/n less than or equal to 1/n and both outer sequences go to 0, we get lim of (sin n)/n = 0. Monotone convergence: the sequence a_n = (1 - 1/n) is increasing and bounded above by 1, so it converges, and its limit is sup {1 - 1/n} = 1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) For epsilon = 0.001, give an N that works for the sequence 1/n. 2) Compute lim of (5 - 2/n). 3) Use the squeeze theorem to find lim of (cos n)/n. 4) Is the sequence a_n = (-1)^n convergent? 5) Compute lim of ((3n^2 + n)/(n^2)). Answers: 1) any N greater than 1000, for instance N = 1001. 2) 5 - 0 = 5. 3) it is squeezed between -1/n and 1/n, so the limit is 0. 4) no; it oscillates between -1 and 1 and never settles inside a small band around a single value. 5) lim of (3 + 1/n) = 3.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: choosing N before epsilon, or letting N depend on n - N must be fixed once epsilon is given. Mistake: applying the quotient limit law when the denominator's limit is 0. Exit: (a) In lim a_n = L, which quantity is chosen first, epsilon or N? (b) A bounded monotone sequence is guaranteed to do what? Answers: epsilon is chosen first, then N is produced from it; it converges (by monotone convergence, a consequence of completeness).

lessons.title: Cauchy sequences and convergence
lessons.grammar_note: In the Cauchy condition both indices m and n roam freely above N - it is |a_m - a_n|, comparing terms to each other, not to a limit L.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the Cauchy criterion, explain why it lets you prove convergence without naming the limit, and use it to show a sequence does or does not converge. Warm-up: can you tell that a sequence settles down without already knowing the number it settles to?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A sequence a_n is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there exists N such that |a_m - a_n| < epsilon for all m, n > N. The point is that the terms bunch together arbitrarily tightly, measured against each other rather than against a limit. The Cauchy criterion, a deep theorem for the reals, states that a sequence of real numbers converges if and only if it is Cauchy. This is enormously useful: you can prove convergence without producing the limit in advance. Its truth again rests on completeness - every real Cauchy sequence is bounded, and completeness supplies the limit. Over the rationals the criterion fails: a sequence of rationals approaching the square root of 2 is Cauchy yet has no rational limit.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: The sequence a_n = 1/n is Cauchy: for m, n > N, |1/m - 1/n| less than or equal to 1/m + 1/n < 2/N, which is below epsilon once N > 2/epsilon. The harmonic partial sums H_n = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n are NOT Cauchy: grouping shows H_{2n} - H_n is at least 1/2 for every n, so the differences do not shrink and the sequence diverges. A slick use of the criterion: if |a_{n+1} - a_n| less than or equal to (1/2)^n, then for m > n the difference telescopes, |a_m - a_n| less than or equal to (1/2)^n + ... + (1/2)^{m-1} < (1/2)^{n-1}, which tends to 0, so the sequence is Cauchy and therefore converges - even though we never named its limit.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) State the Cauchy condition in symbols. 2) Is every convergent sequence Cauchy? 3) Is every Cauchy sequence of real numbers convergent? 4) Why does the harmonic sequence H_n fail to be Cauchy? 5) Over which number system does the Cauchy criterion fail? Answers: 1) for all epsilon > 0 there is N with |a_m - a_n| < epsilon whenever m, n > N. 2) yes, its terms cluster near the common limit. 3) yes, by the Cauchy criterion, which holds because the reals are complete. 4) H_{2n} - H_n is at least 1/2 for all n, so the differences never shrink below epsilon = 1/2. 5) the rationals, which are not complete.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: only checking that consecutive terms |a_{n+1} - a_n| shrink - that alone is not enough (the harmonic sequence has shrinking gaps yet diverges); the condition must hold for all m, n above N. Mistake: thinking Cauchy always implies convergent in every setting; it needs completeness. Exit: (a) A sequence of reals converges if and only if it is what? (b) Give a Cauchy sequence of rationals with no rational limit. Answers: Cauchy; a rational sequence converging to the square root of 2, such as truncated decimals 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, ...

questions.prompt: The supremum of the open interval (0, 1) is...
questions.explanation: 1 is the least upper bound but does not belong to (0, 1), so it is not attained.

questions.prompt: In the definition lim a_n = L, once epsilon is given you must produce...
options: an N so that |a_n - L| < epsilon for all n > N
questions.explanation: You choose N depending on epsilon so the tail stays within the epsilon-band around L.

questions.prompt: To prove lim of 1/n = 0, a valid choice of N given epsilon > 0 is...
questions.explanation: If N > 1/epsilon then for n > N, 1/n < 1/N < epsilon.

questions.prompt: A real sequence converges if and only if it is...
questions.explanation: This is the Cauchy criterion, valid because the reals are complete.

questions.prompt: A bounded monotone sequence of real numbers...
questions.explanation: Monotone convergence follows from completeness; the limit is the sup or inf of the terms.

questions.prompt: The harmonic partial sums H_n = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n...
questions.explanation: H_{2n} - H_n stays at least 1/2, so the sequence is not Cauchy and diverges.

lessons.title: Series and convergence tests
lessons.grammar_note: A series is the limit of its partial sums S_N = a_1 + ... + a_N; 'the series converges' always means 'the sequence S_N converges'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define convergence of an infinite series through its partial sums, apply the divergence, geometric, comparison, and ratio tests, and distinguish absolute from conditional convergence. Warm-up: what is the sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ...?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Given terms a_1, a_2, ..., the series converges to S if the partial sums S_N = a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_N converge to S as N grows. The divergence test is the first filter: if a_n does not tend to 0, the series diverges (the converse fails - terms can go to 0 while the series still diverges, as with the harmonic series). The geometric series with ratio r converges to 1/(1 - r) exactly when |r| < 1. The comparison test bounds a series of nonnegative terms by a known one. The ratio test looks at the limit L of |a_{n+1}/a_n|: if L < 1 the series converges, if L > 1 it diverges, and if L = 1 the test is inconclusive. A series converges absolutely if the sum of |a_n| converges; absolute convergence implies convergence. A series that converges but not absolutely, like the alternating harmonic series, converges conditionally.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Geometric: 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... has r = 1/2, so it sums to 1/(1 - 1/2) = 2. Divergence test: the series with a_n = n/(n+1) diverges because a_n tends to 1, not 0. p-series: 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ... (that is 1/n^2) converges, while 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... (the harmonic series, 1/n) diverges - the borderline is p = 1. Ratio test on 1/n!: the ratio (1/(n+1)!)/(1/n!) = 1/(n+1) tends to 0 < 1, so the sum converges (in fact to e - 1 past the first term). Conditional convergence: 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 + ... converges by the alternating structure, but the sum of absolute values is the divergent harmonic series, so its convergence is only conditional.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Sum the geometric series 1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + .... 2) Does the series with a_n = 1/n^2 converge? 3) Apply the divergence test to a_n = (2n)/(n + 5). 4) Use the ratio test on the series with a_n = 2^n / n!. 5) Does the alternating harmonic series converge absolutely, conditionally, or not at all? Answers: 1) r = 1/3, sum = 1/(1 - 1/3) = 3/2. 2) yes; it is a p-series with p = 2 > 1. 3) a_n tends to 2, not 0, so the series diverges. 4) the ratio (2^{n+1}/(n+1)!)/(2^n/n!) = 2/(n+1) tends to 0 < 1, so it converges. 5) conditionally - it converges, but the harmonic series of absolute values diverges.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: concluding a series converges just because a_n tends to 0 - the harmonic series is the standard counterexample. Mistake: forgetting that the ratio test says nothing when the limit equals 1. Exit: (a) For which r does the geometric series converge? (b) Does absolute convergence imply convergence, or the reverse? Answers: |r| < 1; absolute convergence implies convergence, but not the reverse.

lessons.title: Limits and continuity (epsilon-delta)
lessons.grammar_note: The condition is |x - a| < delta implies |f(x) - f(a)| < epsilon; the input closeness delta responds to the output tolerance epsilon, not the other way around.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write the epsilon-delta definitions of a function limit and of continuity, prove a function is continuous at a point by producing delta from epsilon, and state what uniform continuity adds. Warm-up: to keep 2x within 0.1 of 2a, how close must x be to a?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a equals L if for every epsilon > 0 there is a delta > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < delta implies |f(x) - L| < epsilon. The function f is continuous at a if this holds with L = f(a): for every epsilon > 0 there is delta > 0 with |x - a| < delta implying |f(x) - f(a)| < epsilon. Continuity is preserved by sums, products, quotients (nonzero denominator), and composition. There is also a sequential picture: f is continuous at a exactly when f(x_n) tends to f(a) for every sequence x_n tending to a. Uniform continuity strengthens this by demanding a single delta that works for every point at once, not one delta per point; a key theorem says every continuous function on a closed bounded interval is automatically uniformly continuous.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Continuity of f(x) = 2x at any a: given epsilon > 0, choose delta = epsilon/2. Then |x - a| < delta gives |2x - 2a| = 2|x - a| < 2 delta = epsilon. Continuity of f(x) = x^2 at a = 3: |x^2 - 9| = |x - 3||x + 3|; restricting delta less than or equal to 1 keeps |x + 3| below 7, so choosing delta = min(1, epsilon/7) yields |x^2 - 9| < 7 delta less than or equal to epsilon. A discontinuity: the sign function, which is -1 for x < 0 and 1 for x > 0, has no limit at 0, since sequences approaching 0 from the two sides give different values. Uniform continuity contrast: f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1) is continuous at each point but not uniformly continuous, because the required delta shrinks to 0 as a approaches 0.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) For f(x) = 3x and epsilon = 0.03, what delta makes |3x - 3a| < epsilon? 2) Is f(x) = 5 (constant) continuous everywhere? 3) Give the sequential test for continuity at a. 4) Does f(x) = x^2 satisfy |x^2 - 9| = |x - 3||x + 3|? 5) Name a function continuous on (0, 1) but not uniformly continuous there. Answers: 1) delta = epsilon/3 = 0.01, since |3x - 3a| = 3|x - a| < 3 delta = epsilon. 2) yes; |f(x) - f(a)| = 0 < epsilon for any delta. 3) f(x_n) tends to f(a) for every sequence x_n tending to a. 4) yes, that factoring is exact. 5) f(x) = 1/x.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: swapping the roles of epsilon and delta - epsilon is the output tolerance you are handed, delta is the input closeness you must find. Mistake: assuming pointwise continuity on an open interval gives a single delta for all points; that is uniform continuity, which can fail. Exit: (a) In continuity at a, which is chosen first, epsilon or delta? (b) Every continuous function on a closed bounded interval has what stronger property? Answers: epsilon is given first, then delta is produced; it is uniformly continuous.

lessons.title: The extreme and intermediate value theorems
lessons.grammar_note: Both theorems need a CLOSED and BOUNDED interval [a, b]; drop closedness and f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1] loses its maximum, drop boundedness and the guarantees fail.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the extreme value theorem and the intermediate value theorem, explain why each hypothesis matters, and use them to prove maxima exist and roots exist. Warm-up: if a continuous path starts below sea level and ends above it, must it cross sea level?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The extreme value theorem says that a function continuous on a closed bounded interval [a, b] attains a maximum and a minimum value on that interval - there are points where f reaches its highest and lowest outputs. The intermediate value theorem says that if f is continuous on [a, b] and y is any value between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = y for some c in [a, b]; a continuous function skips no intermediate values. The extreme value theorem rests on two facts: a continuous function on a closed bounded interval is bounded, and the supremum of its values is actually attained. The intermediate value theorem is proved by completeness - take the supremum of all x where f stays below y, and continuity forces f to equal y there. Both hypotheses are essential: continuity and a closed, bounded domain.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Root finding: f(x) = x^2 - 2 is continuous on [1, 2] with f(1) = -1 < 0 and f(2) = 2 > 0. Since 0 lies between them, the intermediate value theorem gives some c in (1, 2) with f(c) = 0 - that c is the square root of 2, proving it exists as a real number. Any odd-degree polynomial has a real root, because it runs from negative values to positive values and continuity forces a crossing. Extreme value theorem in action: f(x) = x^2 on [-1, 3] is continuous on a closed bounded interval, so it attains a max (value 9 at x = 3) and a min (value 0 at x = 0). Why hypotheses matter: f(x) = x on the open interval (0, 1) is continuous but attains neither a max nor a min, since sup = 1 and inf = 0 are never reached - the interval is not closed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Does f(x) = cos x - x have a root in [0, 1]? Explain by sign change. 2) State the two hypotheses the extreme value theorem needs. 3) Why does f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1] have no maximum? 4) Must every cubic polynomial have a real root? 5) Which theorem guarantees a continuous f on [a, b] hits every value between f(a) and f(b)? Answers: 1) yes; at x = 0 the value is 1 > 0 and at x = 1 it is cos 1 - 1 < 0, so a root lies between by the intermediate value theorem. 2) continuity, and a closed bounded interval. 3) as x approaches 0 the values grow without bound, so there is no largest value; the interval is not closed at 0. 4) yes; odd degree forces a sign change, so the intermediate value theorem gives a root. 5) the intermediate value theorem.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: applying the extreme value theorem on an open or unbounded interval, where maxima can fail to exist. Mistake: thinking the intermediate value theorem locates the crossing point - it only guarantees one exists. Exit: (a) On what kind of interval does the extreme value theorem hold? (b) What does a sign change of a continuous f on [a, b] guarantee? Answers: a closed bounded interval; a root, some c with f(c) = 0, by the intermediate value theorem.

questions.prompt: The geometric series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... sums to...
questions.explanation: With r = 1/2 the sum is 1/(1 - 1/2) = 2.

questions.prompt: If the terms a_n do NOT tend to 0, then the series...
questions.explanation: The divergence test: nonzero-limit terms force the partial sums not to settle.

questions.prompt: The alternating harmonic series 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 + ... converges...
questions.explanation: It converges, but the sum of absolute values is the divergent harmonic series, so convergence is conditional.

questions.prompt: To prove f(x) = 2x is continuous at a, given epsilon > 0 a valid delta is...
questions.explanation: |2x - 2a| = 2|x - a| < 2 delta, so delta = epsilon/2 makes this less than epsilon.

questions.prompt: The extreme value theorem guarantees a maximum and minimum when f is continuous on...
questions.explanation: Closed and bounded are both required; drop either and the extremum can fail to exist.

questions.prompt: That f(x) = x^2 - 2 changes sign on [1, 2] proves, via the intermediate value theorem, that...
options: the square root of 2 exists as a real number
questions.explanation: A sign change forces a root c with c^2 = 2, so sqrt(2) is a real number.

lessons.title: Differentiation and the mean value theorem
lessons.grammar_note: Differentiable at a always implies continuous at a, but the reverse fails: f(x) = |x| is continuous at 0 yet has no derivative there.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define the derivative as a limit of difference quotients, show differentiability implies continuity, and state and apply the mean value theorem. Warm-up: what is the average rate of change of f(x) = x^2 from x = 1 to x = 3?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The derivative of f at a is f'(a) = lim of (f(x) - f(a)) / (x - a) as x approaches a, when this limit exists; it is the instantaneous rate of change and the slope of the tangent line. Differentiability at a implies continuity at a, because the difference quotient can only have a limit if f(x) - f(a) tends to 0. The reverse fails, as the corner of |x| at 0 shows. Rolle's theorem is the seed result: if f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then f'(c) = 0 for some c in (a, b). The mean value theorem generalizes it: under the same continuity and differentiability hypotheses, there is a c in (a, b) with f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a) - at some interior point the instantaneous slope equals the average slope across the whole interval. It underlies the facts that a zero derivative means constant and a positive derivative means increasing.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: From the definition, f(x) = x^2 has f'(a) = lim of ((x^2 - a^2)/(x - a)) = lim of (x + a) = 2a. Continuity from differentiability: if f'(a) exists then f(x) - f(a) = ((f(x) - f(a))/(x - a)) times (x - a), and the product tends to f'(a) times 0 = 0, so f(x) tends to f(a). Mean value theorem: on f(x) = x^2 over [1, 3], the average slope is (9 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 4, and setting f'(c) = 2c = 4 gives c = 2, which indeed lies in (1, 3). Consequence: if f'(x) = 0 on an interval, then for any two points the mean value theorem gives f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a) = 0, so f is constant.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Use the definition to find f'(a) for f(x) = 3x. 2) Is f(x) = |x| differentiable at 0? 3) State Rolle's theorem's extra hypothesis beyond the mean value theorem's. 4) For f(x) = x^2 on [0, 4], find the c the mean value theorem provides. 5) If f'(x) > 0 throughout an interval, what can you conclude about f? Answers: 1) lim of ((3x - 3a)/(x - a)) = 3, so f'(a) = 3. 2) no; the left and right difference quotients give -1 and 1, so the limit does not exist. 3) Rolle's adds the condition f(a) = f(b), forcing f'(c) = 0. 4) average slope (16 - 0)/(4 - 0) = 4, and 2c = 4 gives c = 2. 5) f is strictly increasing on that interval.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing continuity implies differentiability; |x| refutes this at 0. Mistake: applying the mean value theorem without checking differentiability on the open interval and continuity on the closed one. Exit: (a) Differentiable at a implies what weaker property? (b) What equation does the c from the mean value theorem satisfy? Answers: continuous at a; f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a).

lessons.title: Riemann integration
lessons.grammar_note: Integrability means the lower and upper sums squeeze to the SAME number as the partition is refined; write the integral as lim of the Riemann sums.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define the Riemann integral through upper and lower sums, use the integrability criterion, and state the fundamental theorem of calculus that links integration to differentiation. Warm-up: how would you trap the area under a curve between two staircase estimates?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Partition [a, b] into subintervals. On each piece, the lower sum uses the infimum of f and the upper sum uses the supremum of f, times the width. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum. The lower integral is the sup of all lower sums; the upper integral is the inf of all upper sums. The function f is Riemann integrable on [a, b] when these two agree, and the common value is the integral. The working criterion: f is integrable exactly when, for every epsilon > 0, there is a partition whose upper sum minus lower sum is less than epsilon. Every continuous function on [a, b] is integrable, and so is every bounded monotone function. The fundamental theorem of calculus ties it together: if F' = f with f continuous, then the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) - F(a); and the function x maps to the integral of f from a to x is an antiderivative of f.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: For f(x) = x on [0, 1], split into n equal pieces of width 1/n. The upper sum is the sum of (k/n)(1/n) for k = 1 to n, which is (1/n^2) times n(n+1)/2 = (n+1)/(2n), tending to 1/2. The lower sum uses k-1 in place of k and tends to 1/2 as well, so the two squeeze to the integral 1/2 - matching the triangle area. A non-integrable example: the function that is 1 on rationals and 0 on irrationals has, on every subinterval, infimum 0 and supremum 1, so its lower integral is 0 and upper integral is 1; they never meet, so it is not Riemann integrable. Fundamental theorem: since F(x) = x^2/2 has F'(x) = x, the integral of x from 0 to 1 is F(1) - F(0) = 1/2 - 0 = 1/2, confirming the sum computation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What two quantities must agree for f to be Riemann integrable? 2) State the epsilon criterion for integrability. 3) Is every continuous function on [a, b] integrable? 4) Using the fundamental theorem, evaluate the integral of x^2 from 0 to 3. 5) Why is the rational-indicator function not Riemann integrable? Answers: 1) the lower integral (sup of lower sums) and the upper integral (inf of upper sums). 2) for every epsilon > 0 there is a partition with upper sum minus lower sum less than epsilon. 3) yes. 4) an antiderivative is x^3/3, so the value is 27/3 - 0 = 9. 5) on every subinterval its inf is 0 and sup is 1, so lower and upper integrals are 0 and (b - a), which never agree.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming every bounded function is integrable - the rational indicator is a bounded counterexample. Mistake: forgetting that the fundamental theorem needs f continuous (and F an antiderivative) to write the integral as F(b) - F(a). Exit: (a) f is integrable when which two integrals coincide? (b) If F' = f is continuous, the integral of f from a to b equals what? Answers: the lower and upper integrals; F(b) - F(a).

lessons.title: Sequences of functions: pointwise versus uniform convergence
lessons.grammar_note: Pointwise: for each x pick N depending on x AND epsilon. Uniform: one N works for ALL x at once, depending on epsilon only - that single N is what preserves continuity in the limit.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish pointwise from uniform convergence of a sequence of functions, test which one holds, and explain why uniform convergence preserves continuity while pointwise convergence need not. Warm-up: can a limit of continuous functions be discontinuous?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A sequence of functions f_n converges pointwise to f on a set if, for each fixed x, the numbers f_n(x) converge to f(x); here the N you need may depend on both x and epsilon. It converges uniformly to f if a single N works for every x simultaneously: for every epsilon > 0 there is N such that |f_n(x) - f(x)| < epsilon for all n > N and all x. The gap between the two is the whole story of the subject. Uniform convergence is governed by the supremum: f_n tends to f uniformly exactly when the sup over x of |f_n(x) - f(x)| tends to 0. Uniform convergence preserves good behavior - the uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, and under uniform convergence you may swap the limit with an integral. Pointwise convergence gives none of these guarantees.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: On [0, 1], f_n(x) = x^n converges pointwise to the function that is 0 for x in [0, 1) and 1 at x = 1. Each f_n is continuous, but the limit jumps at 1, so the convergence cannot be uniform - indeed the sup of |x^n - 0| over [0, 1) stays equal to 1 for every n, never shrinking to 0. Contrast: f_n(x) = x/n on [0, 1] converges to 0 uniformly, since the sup of |x/n| over [0, 1] is 1/n, which tends to 0; here one N = ceil(1/epsilon) works for all x. Preservation: because x/n tends to 0 uniformly and each x/n is continuous, the limit function 0 is continuous, as the theorem promises.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which mode of convergence lets N depend on x? 2) For f_n(x) = x^n on [0, 1], why is the convergence not uniform? 3) Compute the sup of |x/n| over [0, 1] and its limit. 4) What property of continuous functions does uniform convergence preserve? 5) Give the supremum test for uniform convergence. Answers: 1) pointwise convergence. 2) the pointwise limit is discontinuous at x = 1, and the sup of |x^n| over [0, 1) equals 1 for every n, so it does not tend to 0. 3) the sup is 1/n, which tends to 0, giving uniform convergence to 0. 4) continuity of the limit (the uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous). 5) f_n tends to f uniformly exactly when sup over x of |f_n(x) - f(x)| tends to 0.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming pointwise convergence of continuous functions yields a continuous limit - x^n on [0, 1] is the standard counterexample. Mistake: reading off a per-point N and calling the convergence uniform; uniform demands one N for all x. Exit: (a) Which convergence needs a single N for all x? (b) What does the uniform limit of continuous functions inherit? Answers: uniform convergence; continuity.

questions.prompt: The derivative of f at a is defined as the limit of...
options: (f(x) - f(a)) / (x - a) as x approaches a
the average of f on [a, x]
questions.explanation: The derivative is the limit of difference quotients, when it exists.

questions.prompt: Which implication is always true?
options: continuous at a implies differentiable at a
differentiable at a implies continuous at a
questions.explanation: Differentiability forces continuity; the converse fails, as |x| at 0 shows.

questions.prompt: The mean value theorem provides a point c in (a, b) where f'(c) equals...
questions.explanation: The instantaneous slope at c matches the average slope across [a, b].

questions.prompt: A function f is Riemann integrable on [a, b] when...
options: its lower and upper integrals are equal
questions.explanation: Integrability means the sup of lower sums equals the inf of upper sums.

questions.prompt: The uniform limit of continuous functions is...
questions.explanation: Uniform convergence preserves continuity of the limit function.

questions.prompt: The sequence f_n(x) = x^n on [0, 1] converges...
options: pointwise to a discontinuous limit, not uniformly
questions.explanation: The pointwise limit jumps at x = 1, and the sup of |x^n| over [0, 1) stays 1, so convergence is not uniform.

lessons.title: Capstone proof set: assembling the machinery
lessons.grammar_note: Every proof here traces back to completeness - the least-upper-bound property is the single axiom that powers convergence, continuity theorems, and integrability.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write complete, rigorous proofs that stitch the course together: bound-to-supremum arguments, epsilon-N and epsilon-delta constructions, and applications of the big theorems. Warm-up: which single property of the reals keeps reappearing under every major theorem so far?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Real analysis is a small number of tools used repeatedly. Completeness supplies suprema and infima, which power the monotone convergence theorem, the Cauchy criterion, the extreme value theorem, the intermediate value theorem, and Riemann integrability. The epsilon-N template proves statements about sequences; the epsilon-delta template proves statements about limits and continuity. Structuring a proof means: state exactly what is given and what must be shown, name the tolerance (epsilon) the adversary hands you, construct the response (N or delta) explicitly from it, and verify the required inequality. A capstone habit is to name which theorem or axiom licenses each step, so the logical spine is visible from base case to conclusion.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Proof (bounded + monotone converges): let a_n be increasing and bounded above. By completeness the set {a_n} has a supremum L. Given epsilon > 0, since L - epsilon is not an upper bound, some a_N exceeds L - epsilon; by monotonicity a_n is at least a_N > L - epsilon for all n > N, and a_n less than or equal to L always, so |a_n - L| < epsilon. Hence a_n tends to L. Proof (a continuous function on [0, 1] with f(0) < 0 < f(1) has a root): f is continuous on a closed bounded interval and 0 lies between f(0) and f(1), so by the intermediate value theorem there is c in (0, 1) with f(c) = 0. Proof (product of convergent sequences): if a_n tends to A and b_n tends to B, then a_n b_n tends to AB, shown by writing a_n b_n - AB = a_n(b_n - B) + B(a_n - A), bounding |a_n| since convergent sequences are bounded, and driving each piece below epsilon/2.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which axiom guarantees the supremum L exists in the monotone convergence proof? 2) In the root-existence proof, which theorem is invoked and which hypothesis on the interval does it require? 3) In the product proof, why is |a_n| bounded? 4) Prove that a decreasing sequence bounded below converges, by analogy. 5) What does naming the licensing theorem at each step buy you? Answers: 1) completeness, the least-upper-bound property. 2) the intermediate value theorem, which requires f continuous on a closed bounded interval. 3) convergent sequences are bounded, so |a_n| stays below some fixed M. 4) by completeness the terms have an infimum L; given epsilon > 0, some a_N < L + epsilon, and monotonicity keeps a_n within (L, L + epsilon) for n > N, so a_n tends to L. 5) it makes the logical spine explicit and shows every step is justified rather than assumed.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: invoking a theorem whose hypotheses you have not checked, such as the intermediate value theorem without continuity on a closed interval. Mistake: writing 'clearly it converges' instead of constructing N or delta from epsilon. Exit: (a) Which single axiom underlies monotone convergence, the Cauchy criterion, and the extreme value theorem? (b) In an epsilon-delta proof, what must you build explicitly from the given epsilon? Answers: completeness (the least-upper-bound property); a delta that makes the required inequality hold.

questions.prompt: The completeness axiom states that every nonempty set of reals bounded above has...
questions.explanation: The least-upper-bound property guarantees a real supremum; it need not be a maximum.

questions.prompt: To prove M = sup S you must show M is an upper bound and that...
options: for every epsilon > 0 some x in S exceeds M - epsilon
questions.explanation: The second property says nothing smaller than M can be an upper bound.

questions.prompt: A real sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy; this relies on the reals being...
questions.explanation: Completeness supplies the limit of every Cauchy sequence; over the rationals the criterion fails.

questions.prompt: The series with terms 1/n^2 (n = 1, 2, 3, ...)...
options: converges, as a p-series with p = 2
questions.explanation: It is a p-series with p = 2 > 1, so it converges.

questions.prompt: In the epsilon-delta definition of continuity at a, delta is chosen...
options: in response to a given epsilon
questions.explanation: Epsilon (output tolerance) is handed to you first; you then produce delta (input closeness).

questions.prompt: The intermediate value theorem lets you conclude the square root of 2 exists because x^2 - 2...
questions.explanation: A continuous sign change forces a root c with c^2 = 2.

questions.prompt: The extreme value theorem needs the domain to be...
questions.explanation: Both closedness and boundedness are required for the max and min to be attained.

questions.prompt: The mean value theorem guarantees a c in (a, b) with f'(c) equal to...
questions.explanation: The instantaneous slope at c equals the average slope over [a, b].

questions.prompt: The function that is 1 on rationals and 0 on irrationals is not Riemann integrable because...
options: on every subinterval its inf is 0 and sup is 1, so lower and upper integrals differ
questions.explanation: The lower integral is 0 and the upper integral is (b - a); they never agree.

questions.prompt: By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the integral of x from 0 to 1 equals...
questions.explanation: An antiderivative is x^2/2, so the value is 1/2 - 0 = 1/2.

questions.prompt: The uniform limit of continuous functions is guaranteed to be...
questions.explanation: Uniform convergence preserves continuity; pointwise convergence does not.

questions.prompt: For f_n(x) = x^n on [0, 1], the convergence is not uniform because...
options: the sup of |x^n| over [0, 1) stays equal to 1 for every n
questions.explanation: The supremum of the error does not tend to 0, and the pointwise limit jumps at x = 1.
